Key Ideas & Details.q: In reading, what is the main idea of a passage?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The author's central point about the topic, in a complete sentence
Key Ideas & Details.w: The main idea is the point the author makes about the topic, expressed as a full sentence ("Vaccines prevent disease by training the immune system").

Key Ideas & Details.q: Where is a stated main idea most often found?
Key Ideas & Details.a: In a topic sentence, often first or last in a paragraph
Key Ideas & Details.w: A stated main idea usually appears in a topic sentence at the start or end of a paragraph, or in the thesis at the end of an introduction. When it is implied, the reader combines the paragraph's points.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Which description best fits a supporting detail?
Key Ideas & Details.a: A fact, example or reason that backs up the main idea
Key Ideas & Details.w: Supporting details (facts, examples, statistics, reasons, anecdotes) explain or prove the main idea.

Key Ideas & Details.q: What should a good summary of a passage include?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The main idea and key supporting points, in the original order
Key Ideas & Details.w: A summary is a brief, objective restatement in your own words of the main idea and the most important supporting points, in the same order and with the same emphasis as the original.

Key Ideas & Details.q: How does a summary differ from a paraphrase?
Key Ideas & Details.a: A summary is shorter; a paraphrase is about the same length
Key Ideas & Details.w: Both restate ideas in your own words. A paraphrase restates a specific passage at about the same length; a summary condenses the main idea and key points into a shorter version.

Key Ideas & Details.q: An answer option accurately restates the first paragraph of a three-paragraph passage. Why is it a weak summary?
Key Ideas & Details.a: A summary must cover the whole text, not one part
Key Ideas & Details.w: A good summary covers all paragraphs. An option that restates only the first (or last) paragraph is a classic trap in summary questions.

Key Ideas & Details.q: In a reading question, what is an inference?
Key Ideas & Details.a: A conclusion based on text evidence plus reasoning
Key Ideas & Details.w: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from evidence in the text combined with reasoning; it is not stated directly, but the text supports it.

Key Ideas & Details.q: When several inferences seem possible, which one should you choose?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The one most strongly supported by the text
Key Ideas & Details.w: The best inference is the one that must be true or is most strongly supported by details in the passage.

Key Ideas & Details.q: A question asks why an author included a particular detail. What is it testing?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Inferring the detail's purpose in the text
Key Ideas & Details.w: Why a detail, example or paragraph was included is an inference about purpose and meaning: what the detail contributes (to illustrate, to give evidence, to engage the reader).

Key Ideas & Details.q: What separates an inference from an assumption?
Key Ideas & Details.a: An inference is supported by the text; an assumption is not
Key Ideas & Details.w: An inference is a conclusion reached from text evidence plus reasoning. An assumption is an unsupported belief the reader brings to the text.

Key Ideas & Details.q: In inference questions, why are options with words such as all, proves or every often wrong?
Key Ideas & Details.a: They usually claim more than the evidence supports
Key Ideas & Details.w: Extreme wording overreaches: the best inference is the one the text most strongly supports, and sweeping claims rarely have that support.

Key Ideas & Details.q: A passage reports that two things tend to occur together. What can a reader safely conclude?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The two are linked, but cause is unproven
Key Ideas & Details.w: Two things occurring together shows a correlation. Without more evidence, the reader cannot conclude that either one causes the other.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Directions say, "Take the missed dose, unless the next dose is due within 4 hours." What does unless signal?
Key Ideas & Details.a: A condition that cancels the instruction when it is met
Key Ideas & Details.w: "Unless" introduces an exception: if the condition is true, the instruction does not apply. Ignoring "unless" or "except" conditions is a common direction-following error.

Key Ideas & Details.q: A step in a set of directions applies only if a condition is met. What should you do when the condition is not met?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Skip that step and continue with the next
Key Ideas & Details.w: A conditional step is performed only when its condition is true; otherwise you skip it and continue in order.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Directions say, "Seal the tube in the bag, but first wrap it in the pad." Which action comes first?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Wrapping the tube in the pad
Key Ideas & Details.w: "But first" moves the wrapping ahead of the sealing. Order of mention is not always the order of action, so watch for before, after and first.

Key Ideas & Details.q: In a multi-step direction puzzle, each step should be applied to what?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The result produced by the step just before it
Key Ideas & Details.w: Each step acts on the result of the previous step. Applying a step to the original item is one of the most common errors.

Key Ideas & Details.q: What is the safest way to work through a direction puzzle with five or more steps?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Write down the result after every single step
Key Ideas & Details.w: Writing each intermediate state prevents skipped steps, off-by-one position errors and stopping one step early.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Start with PLANET and remove the second letter. Which letter is now in the third position?
Key Ideas & Details.a: N
Key Ideas & Details.w: Removing L leaves PANET, so the third letter is N. Positions shift after a deletion, so recount from the new word.

Key Ideas & Details.q: What is scanning?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Searching quickly for a specific word, number or name
Key Ideas & Details.w: Scanning means moving quickly through a text to find a specific item, such as a date, name, figure or keyword.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Which text features help a reader find specific information quickly?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Headings, bold words and captions
Key Ideas & Details.w: Text features such as titles, headings, subheadings, bold or italic words, lists, captions, sidebars, glossaries and indexes point the reader to specific information.

Key Ideas & Details.q: A question begins "According to the passage." What should the answer be based on?
Key Ideas & Details.a: What the passage actually states
Key Ideas & Details.w: "According to the passage" asks for information stated in the text. An option can be true in the real world and still be wrong if the passage does not say it.

Key Ideas & Details.q: On a Nutrition Facts label, the amounts listed for calories and nutrients apply to what?
Key Ideas & Details.a: One serving
Key Ideas & Details.w: Label amounts and % Daily Values are per serving. Multiply by the number of servings eaten to find the total.

Key Ideas & Details.q: How does a table of contents differ from an index?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Contents: front of book, in page order; index: back, alphabetical
Key Ideas & Details.w: A table of contents is at the front and lists chapters and sections in order with starting pages. An index is at the back and lists specific topics alphabetically with every page where each appears.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Which line of a memo most directly tells the reader its topic?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The Subject (Re) line
Key Ideas & Details.w: The Subject or Re line states what the memo is about. To, From and Date identify the audience, sender and timing.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Before reading values from a graph, what should you check first?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The title, axis labels, units and scale
Key Ideas & Details.w: The title, axis labels, units (for example, thousands) and scale tell you what each value means. Misreading the scale or units is a top graph trap.

Key Ideas & Details.q: On a pie chart, what does each section represent?
Key Ideas & Details.a: A part's percentage share of the whole
Key Ideas & Details.w: Pie chart sections show parts of a whole, usually as percentages. To get a count, multiply the percentage by the total.

Key Ideas & Details.q: A map's scale is 1 inch = 20 miles. Two towns are 2.5 inches apart on the map. How far apart are they?
Key Ideas & Details.a: 50 miles
Key Ideas & Details.w: Multiply map distance by the scale: 2.5 x 20 = 50 miles.

Key Ideas & Details.q: A passage describes events out of order. A sequence question asks you to track which order?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The order in which events actually happened
Key Ideas & Details.w: Sequence questions ask about the order of occurrence. Flashbacks and summaries can mention later events first, so use dates and signal words.

Key Ideas & Details.q: Which signal word shows that two events happened at the same time?
Key Ideas & Details.a: Meanwhile
Key Ideas & Details.w: Meanwhile (like while, during and simultaneously) signals events happening at the same time.

Key Ideas & Details.q: "By the time the doctor arrived, the nurse had started the IV." Which event happened first?
Key Ideas & Details.a: The nurse started the IV
Key Ideas & Details.w: "By the time" plus the past perfect "had started" means the IV was started before the doctor arrived.

Craft & Structure.q: A brochure states, "Our county has 14 hospitals," but the county actually has 11. How is the brochure's statement classified?
Craft & Structure.a: A factual claim that is false
Craft & Structure.w: A fact is a statement that can be checked and proven true or false. This one can be checked, and it turns out to be false, so it is a false factual claim, not an opinion.

Craft & Structure.q: A cardiologist with 30 years of experience writes, "A Mediterranean diet is the best eating plan for heart health." How should a reader classify this statement?
Craft & Structure.a: An opinion, even though an expert made it
Craft & Structure.w: "The best eating plan" is a judgment. An expert's opinion is more credible than a stranger's, but it is still an opinion.

Craft & Structure.q: Which word in a sentence most often signals that the sentence is an opinion?
Craft & Structure.w: "Should" expresses what the writer thinks ought to happen, which is a judgment others may not share.

Craft & Structure.q: A one-sided presentation that favors a viewpoint, often by using loaded words or leaving out opposing evidence, is called what?
Craft & Structure.w: Bias is a slant toward one side, shown through loaded language, omitted counterevidence, cherry-picked data or unequal treatment of the sides.

Craft & Structure.q: "Teenagers are too glued to their phones to hold a real conversation." This sentence is best described as which of the following?
Craft & Structure.w: The sentence applies one oversimplified trait to every teenager. A generalization about an entire group is a stereotype.

Craft & Structure.q: A belief that many people hold but that evidence shows to be incorrect is called what?
Craft & Structure.w: A misconception is a commonly held but incorrect belief. Passages often name one ("Many people think...") and then correct it with evidence.

Craft & Structure.q: Which signal word most often introduces a contrast (antonym) context clue?
Craft & Structure.w: "However" (like but, unlike, whereas and although) signals that the unknown word means something opposite to a nearby idea.

Craft & Structure.q: "The patient saw a nephrologist, or kidney specialist, every month." Which type of context clue explains the word nephrologist?
Craft & Structure.w: The phrase set off by "or" and commas renames the word directly, which is a definition or restatement clue.

Craft & Structure.q: Which phrase signals an example context clue?
Craft & Structure.w: "For instance" (like such as, including and for example) introduces examples that show what the unknown word covers.

Craft & Structure.q: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word, apart from any feelings attached to it, is called its what?
Craft & Structure.w: Denotation is a word's literal dictionary meaning.

Craft & Structure.q: Which word describes the same behavior as "nosy" but with a positive connotation?
Craft & Structure.w: "Curious" names an interest in learning about others, with the positive sense of healthy interest.

Craft & Structure.q: An author's attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice, is called what?
Craft & Structure.w: Tone is the author's attitude (for example skeptical, admiring or indignant), created by word choice and detail.

Craft & Structure.q: A figure of speech that compares two unlike things using "like" or "as" is called what?
Craft & Structure.w: A simile makes its comparison with "like" or "as": "The waiting room was as quiet as a library."

Craft & Structure.q: A brief reference to a well-known person, place, event or literary work, such as calling a difficult task "a Herculean effort," is called what?
Craft & Structure.w: An allusion points to something the reader is expected to recognize; "Herculean" refers to the hero Hercules and his famous labors.

Craft & Structure.q: Which phrase is an example of onomatopoeia?
Craft & Structure.a: the buzz of the fluorescent lights
Craft & Structure.w: Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates the sound it names. "Buzz" sounds like the noise the lights make.

Craft & Structure.q: A newspaper editorial urges readers to vote yes on a school bond. What is its most likely primary purpose?
Craft & Structure.w: Editorials argue a position and often end with a call to action, such as voting yes; that is a persuasive purpose.

Craft & Structure.q: An informational article about food allergies opens with a short story about a child's reaction at a birthday party. What is the most likely purpose of this opening?
Craft & Structure.a: to engage the reader before the information begins
Craft & Structure.w: An anecdote at the start of an informational text draws the reader in and introduces the topic; the purpose of the whole article is still to inform.

Craft & Structure.q: A writer tries to persuade by appealing to the reader's feelings, such as fear, pity or pride. What is this type of appeal called?
Craft & Structure.w: Pathos is an appeal to emotion.

Craft & Structure.q: Which set of signal words most often marks a compare-and-contrast structure?
Craft & Structure.w: "Similarly" signals a likeness, and "unlike" and "whereas" signal differences, which together mark compare and contrast.

Craft & Structure.q: A passage first describes a shortage of nurses in rural hospitals and then explains three programs designed to address it. Which structure does it use?
Craft & Structure.w: A passage that presents a challenge and then explains ways to address it uses problem-and-solution structure.

Craft & Structure.q: Printed instructions for assembling a folding wheelchair are an example of which type of text?
Craft & Structure.w: Technical texts give precise, often numbered directions for completing a task or using equipment.

Craft & Structure.q: A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of every character is using which point of view?
Craft & Structure.w: "Omniscient" means all-knowing; this narrator can reveal any character's inner thoughts.

Craft & Structure.q: A story is told by a character who says "I" and takes part in the events. Inside the story, other characters often say "you" to the narrator. What is the story's point of view?
Craft & Structure.w: The narrator's own pronoun decides point of view. A narrator who is a character and speaks as "I" is first person, whatever pronouns appear in dialogue.

Craft & Structure.q: A writer presents only verifiable facts, gives each side equal space and avoids judgment words. How would this text be described?
Craft & Structure.w: Objective writing is neutral and balanced and keeps the author's feelings out of the text.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: When a question asks which sentence best supports a conclusion, the best choice is the sentence that
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: directly shows that the conclusion is true
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: The best evidence directly proves the specific claim. A sentence can be on topic yet support a different claim.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A conclusion drawn from a passage is well supported when it
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: is consistent with every relevant detail in the passage
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A supported conclusion fits all the relevant details and contradicts none; it comes from the text, not from outside knowledge.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A passage reports better results for people who chose to join a program. Why is "the program caused the better results" a weak conclusion?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: People who chose to join may differ from others
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: When people choose to join, they may already differ (for example, more motivated), so the passage shows a link, not cause.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: On the TEAS, a prediction about a passage is best supported when it
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: follows from patterns or causes stated in the passage
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Good predictions extend what the text establishes: stated trends, causes in motion, character traits and foreshadowing.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A table shows a clinic's patient count rising by about 100 each year for four years. Which prediction over-extends the data?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: The count will rise by about 400 next year
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: The pattern is about 100 a year; a jump of about 400 in one year goes far beyond the trend with no stated cause.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: In a story, a hint about events that will happen later is called
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: foreshadowing
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Foreshadowing plants clues about later events, so it is a key source of evidence for predictions.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Which of these is stated as a theme rather than a topic?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: True friends can survive honest disagreement
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A theme is a message about life expressed as a complete statement.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: When a question asks for a theme shared by two passages, the correct answer must be
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: supported by both of the passages
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A shared theme has to be supported by each passage. The classic trap is a theme true of only one of them.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Two authors write about the same policy, one calmly and one angrily. What does the difference in tone tell you?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: Agreement must be judged from their claims
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Tone shows attitude, not position. Authors with very different tones can support the same idea, so compare what each one claims.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: In a pair of passages, a shared assumption is
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: an idea both authors take for granted
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A shared assumption is an unstated belief both arguments depend on, such as that a goal is worth pursuing even when they disagree on the method.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A question asks how the author of Passage 2 would respond to Passage 1. Where is the answer found?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: In Passage 2's own claims and reasons
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Predict the response from Passage 2's own position and reasons, then match it to the claim in Passage 1.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Two passages cite the same survey figure but reach opposite conclusions about it. They disagree about the survey's
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: interpretation
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: When both authors accept the same data but draw different meanings from it, the disagreement is one of interpretation.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: In an argument, a counterclaim is
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: an opposing view that the author addresses
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A counterclaim is the other side's position. Strong arguments raise it and answer it with a rebuttal.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: An author persuades by citing statistics and logical reasoning. This appeal is called
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: logos
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Logos appeals to logic through facts, data and reasoning.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A rebuttal in an argument is
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: the author's answer to an opposing view
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A rebuttal responds to a counterclaim, showing why the opposing view does not defeat the author's claim.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A speaker offers one patient's recovery story as proof that a treatment works for everyone. This fallacy is
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: anecdotal evidence
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Anecdotal evidence treats a personal story as proof. One case cannot show what happens across a population.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Which fallacy attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument itself?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: Ad hominem
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Ad hominem (Latin for "to the person") targets the arguer's character or background.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Post hoc reasoning assumes that
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: an earlier event caused a later one
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Post hoc ("after this, therefore because of this") treats sequence in time as proof of cause.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Evidence is sufficient when it
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: is enough to justify the claim being made
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Sufficiency is about quantity and scope: enough support for the claim, not one anecdote or a tiny sample.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A writer claims that a new policy caused a drop in complaints. Which finding would most weaken that claim?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: Another change took effect at the same time
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: An alternative explanation that occurred at the same time weakens a causal claim.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A study praising a product was paid for by the company that makes it. This mainly raises a question about the study's
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: credibility
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A financial interest in the result is a conflict of interest, which lowers credibility.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: An encyclopedia entry is classified as a
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: tertiary source
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Encyclopedias, dictionaries, almanacs and handbooks compile and condense other sources, so they are tertiary.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A review article that summarizes many published studies on one topic is a
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: secondary source
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A review analyzes and summarizes other researchers' studies, so it is secondary. An article reporting the authors' own study is primary.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: When judging a source's credibility, currency refers to
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: how recent the information is
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Currency is the date of the information. Health guidance in particular should be recent.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: Two sources report different figures on the same topic. What should a reader check first?
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: Whether they use the same dates, groups, and definitions
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Differences often come from different time periods, populations or definitions rather than from an error in either source.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A passage gives a monthly total, and a chart gives weekly totals. Before comparing them, you should
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: convert both to the same time unit
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Integrating data with mismatched units or time periods is a common trap; put both on the same basis first.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: On a pie chart from a survey, a slice labeled 25% tells you
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: the share of the whole in that category
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. To get a count, multiply the percentage by the total surveyed.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: To learn what a historical figure personally thought about an event, the best source is usually
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: the person's own letters or diaries
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: A person's own letters and diaries are primary sources that record their views in their own words.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: For the correct dose of an over-the-counter medicine, the best source is
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: the product's current label or insert
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: The current label or insert is specific to that product and its strength, and it is authoritative.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q: A tertiary source such as an encyclopedia is most useful when you need
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.a: a quick overview of a new topic
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Tertiary sources condense information into brief overviews, ideal for background before deeper research.

Numbers & Operations.q: Which percent is equivalent to the fraction 1/6?
How do you change a decimal to a percent?
Numbers & Operations.a: Multiply by 100 and add a percent sign
Numbers & Operations.w: Percent means per hundred, so multiply by 100 (move the decimal point 2 places right): 0.42 = 42%.

Numbers & Operations.q: Which fraction in lowest terms is equal to 0.125?
Numbers & Operations.w: 0.125 = 125/1,000; dividing both terms by 125 gives 1/8.

Numbers & Operations.q: How do you rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction?
Numbers & Operations.a: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator
Numbers & Operations.w: Whole number × denominator + numerator, over the same denominator: 3 2/5 = (15 + 2)/5 = 17/5.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is 56/72 in lowest terms?
Numbers & Operations.w: The GCF of 56 and 72 is 8: 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 72 ÷ 8 = 9, so 7/9.

Numbers & Operations.q: Which mixed number is equal to 29/6?
Numbers & Operations.w: 29 ÷ 6 = 4 with a remainder of 5, so 29/6 = 4 5/6.

Numbers & Operations.q: Dividing by a fraction gives the same result as which operation?
Numbers & Operations.a: Multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor
Numbers & Operations.w: Keep, change, flip: a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c. Only the divisor (the second fraction) is flipped.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is 1/3 + 1/4?
What is 2 1/2 × 4?
What is 0.4 × 0.03?
Numbers & Operations.w: 4 × 3 = 12, and the factors have 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places, so 0.012.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is the first step when dividing by a decimal such as 0.25?
Numbers & Operations.a: Shift both decimal points right until the divisor is whole
Numbers & Operations.w: Move the divisor's decimal point to make it a whole number and move the dividend's the same number of places: 3 ÷ 0.25 = 300 ÷ 25 = 12.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is 4 - 1.35?
Numbers & Operations.w: Write 4 as 4.00 and borrow: 4.00 - 1.35 = 2.65.

Numbers & Operations.q: In the order of operations, what comes right after parentheses and exponents?
Numbers & Operations.a: Multiplication and division, left to right
Numbers & Operations.w: Multiplication and division have equal rank and are done left to right, followed by addition and subtraction left to right.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is -8 - (-3)?
Numbers & Operations.w: Subtracting a negative is adding: -8 + 3 = -5.
2 × 3 × 4 × 1 = 24, and four negative factors (an even number) give a positive product: 24.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is the value of any nonzero number raised to the power 0?
Numbers & Operations.w: a⁰ = 1 for any a that is not 0 (for example 7⁰ = 1).

Numbers & Operations.q: Which expression is equal to a⁻ⁿ (a not 0)?
Numbers & Operations.w: A negative exponent means the reciprocal of the positive power: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ (2⁻³ = 1/8).

Numbers & Operations.q: How is 0.00052 written in scientific notation?
Numbers & Operations.w: Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 5.2, so the exponent is -4.

Numbers & Operations.q: What does ascending order mean?
Numbers & Operations.w: Ascending order goes up: least to greatest. Descending goes down: greatest to least.

Numbers & Operations.q: Which number is greatest: -1/3, -1/2, -3/4 or -2/3?
Numbers & Operations.w: For negative numbers, the one closest to 0 is greatest: -1/3 ≈ -0.33.

Numbers & Operations.q: Which decimal is greatest: 0.29, 0.3, 0.299 or 0.2999?
Numbers & Operations.w: Add zeros to compare: 0.3000 > 0.2999 > 0.2990 > 0.2900. More digits do not make a decimal larger.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is the absolute value of a number?
Numbers & Operations.a: Its distance from 0 on the number line
Numbers & Operations.w: Absolute value is distance from 0, so it is 0 or positive: |-6| = 6 and |6| = 6.

Numbers & Operations.q: On a horizontal number line, in which direction do values increase?
Numbers & Operations.w: Values increase to the right, so -2 is greater than -5 because it is farther right.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is |-5| - |3|?
What is 6.0549 rounded to the nearest hundredth?
Numbers & Operations.w: Look only at the thousandths digit: 4, so keep the hundredths digit 5: 6.05.

Numbers & Operations.q: In which situation should a decimal answer be rounded up to the next whole number?
Numbers & Operations.a: Buses needed to carry a group
Numbers & Operations.w: Round up when you need enough to cover everything (buses, boxes, cans of paint). Round down when only complete units count.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is 0.0849 rounded to the nearest hundredth?
Numbers & Operations.w: The thousandths digit is 4, so keep the hundredths digit 8: 0.08.

Numbers & Operations.q: What is the elapsed time from 2:45 p.m. to 5:10 p.m.?
Numbers & Operations.w: 2:45 to 4:45 is 2 hours; 4:45 to 5:10 is 25 minutes. Total: 2 h 25 min.

Numbers & Operations.q: A word problem asks how many full doses are in a supply. How should a decimal result be handled?
Numbers & Operations.w: Only complete doses count, so round down (13.6 doses → 13 full doses).

Numbers & Operations.q: What is 1430 on the 24-hour clock in 12-hour time?
Numbers & Operations.w: Subtract 12 from hours after 1200: 14 - 12 = 2, so 1430 is 2:30 p.m.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Which expression means '7 less than a number n'?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: 'Less than' reverses the order of the words: start with n and subtract 7, giving n - 7.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Which expression means 'twice the sum of x and 5'?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Form the sum first, (x + 5), then double it: 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: In the cost model C = 12n + 30, what does the 30 represent?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.a: The fixed charge paid before any items
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: In total = rate × quantity + fixed amount, the constant term (30) is the starting or fixed charge, and the coefficient (12) is the cost per item.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: After adding 7 to both sides of 3x - 7 = 11, which equation remains?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Adding 7 undoes the -7: 3x - 7 + 7 = 11 + 7, so 3x = 18. Dividing by 3 then gives x = 6.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Distributing correctly, 5(x - 4) equals:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: The distributive property multiplies every term inside the parentheses: 5 × x - 5 × 4 = 5x - 20.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Solving d = rt for r gives:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: r is multiplied by t, so divide both sides by t: d/t = r.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: What is the least common denominator used to clear the fractions in x/4 + x/6 = 5?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: The least common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12. Multiplying every term by 12 gives 3x + 2x = 60.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Solve: 0.3x = 4.5
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Divide both sides by 0.3. Move both decimal points one place right: 45 ÷ 3 = 15.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: An equation such as 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 has how many solutions?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Distributing gives 2x + 6 = 2x + 6, a true statement for every x, so there are infinitely many solutions.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: In a word problem, 'no more than' translates to which symbol?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: 'No more than 6' means 6 or less, so the symbol is ≤ (less than or equal to).

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Dividing both sides of -5x ≤ 20 by -5 gives:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: 20 ÷ (-5) = -4, and dividing by a negative reverses ≤ to ≥: x ≥ -4.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: A staffing rule needs more than 3 but no more than 6 RNs on a unit. Which inequality fits the number of RNs, n?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: 'More than 3' gives 3 < n; 'no more than 6' gives n ≤ 6. Together: 3 < n ≤ 6.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: To find what percent 18 is of 72, calculate:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Percent = part ÷ whole × 100. 18 ÷ 72 = 0.25, so 18 is 25% of 72.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: 45 is 18% of what number? The calculation is:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Whole = part ÷ percent: 45 ÷ 0.18 = 250.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: What is 150% of 40?
In the percent change formula, the amount of change is divided by which value?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Percent change = (new - original) ÷ original × 100.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: A 20% discount followed by a 10% discount equals a single discount of:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the final price is 72% of the original: a 28% total discount.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: A price after a 25% discount is $60. The original price is found by calculating:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: $60 is 75% of the original, so original = 60 ÷ 0.75 = $80.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: In a group, the ratio of boys to girls is 2:3. What fraction of the group is girls?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Total parts = 2 + 3 = 5. Girls are 3 of the 5 parts, so 3/5 of the group.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: What is the rate of change between the points (2, 10) and (6, 22)?
A unit rate expresses a quantity per:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: A unit rate has a denominator of 1, such as $1.50 per pound or 60 miles per hour.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Cross-multiplying a/b = c/d gives:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Multiply each numerator by the opposite denominator: a × d = b × c.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: If 5 notebooks cost $8.75, how much do 8 notebooks cost at the same price?
In an inverse proportion, if one quantity triples, the other quantity:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: In an inverse proportion xy = k. If x triples, y must become one-third as large to keep the product the same.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: In the dosage formula (D ÷ H) × Q, what does H stand for?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.a: The dose on hand, as labeled
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: D = desired (ordered) dose, H = dose on hand (strength available), Q = quantity that contains H. Example: 375 mg ÷ 250 mg × 5 mL = 7.5 mL.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: A drawing uses a scale of 1 inch : 8 feet. A wall is 3.5 inches long on the drawing. How long is the actual wall?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Each inch represents 8 feet: 3.5 × 8 = 28 feet.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: Doubling every length in a scale drawing multiplies the area by:
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Area scales by the square of the scale factor: 2² = 4.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: A word problem asks how many full doses a bottle provides, and the division gives 16.8. What is the answer?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: When only complete units count (full doses, full rows, items you can afford), round down: 16 doses.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: When a word problem asks 'how many more,' which operation answers it?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: 'How many more' (or 'how many fewer') compares two amounts by subtraction: larger - smaller.

Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.q: A repair service charges a $25 fee plus $9 per hour. Which expression gives the cost for h hours?
Algebra, Percentages & Proportions.w: Total = rate × quantity + fixed amount = 9h + 25.

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many micrograms (mcg) are in 1 milligram (mg)?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg, just as 1 g = 1,000 mg.

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many deciliters (dL) are in 1 liter (L)?
Measurement & Geometry.w: Deci- means one tenth, so 1 L = 10 dL.

Measurement & Geometry.q: To convert a mass from grams to milligrams, what should you do?
Measurement & Geometry.w: Going to a smaller unit gives a larger number: 1 g = 1,000 mg, so multiply by 1,000.

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many fluid ounces are in 1 quart?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 qt = 2 pints = 4 cups = 4 × 8 = 32 fl oz.

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many feet are in 1 mile?
How many pounds are in 1 US (short) ton?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 short ton = 2,000 lb.

Measurement & Geometry.q: Exactly how many centimeters are in 1 inch?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 in = 2.54 cm exactly (25.4 mm).

Measurement & Geometry.q: To change a weight in pounds to kilograms, what should you do?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 kg = 2.2 lb, and a kilogram is the larger unit, so the number of kilograms is smaller: divide pounds by 2.2.

Measurement & Geometry.q: About how many kilometers are in 1 mile?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 mi is about 1.6 km (more precisely 1.609 km).

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many teaspoons equal 1 tablespoon?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 tbsp = 3 tsp (15 mL = 3 × 5 mL).

Measurement & Geometry.q: Normal body temperature of 37 °C is equal to what temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?
Which formula converts a Fahrenheit temperature to Celsius?
Which formula gives the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides b1 and b2 and height h?
Measurement & Geometry.w: Average the two parallel sides and multiply by the perpendicular height: A = 1/2(b1 + b2)h.

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many square feet are in 1 square yard?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 yd² = 3 ft × 3 ft = 9 ft².

Measurement & Geometry.q: In the triangle area formula A = 1/2 × b × h, the height h must be:
Measurement & Geometry.w: The height is the perpendicular (right-angle) distance from the base to the opposite vertex.

Measurement & Geometry.q: Which formula gives the circumference of a circle with diameter d?
Measurement & Geometry.w: C = πd, which is the same as 2πr because d = 2r.

Measurement & Geometry.q: Which formula gives the area of a circle with radius r?
Measurement & Geometry.w: A = πr², measured in square units.

Measurement & Geometry.q: A circle has a diameter of 18 centimeters. What is its radius?
Which formula gives the volume of a cylinder with radius r and height h?
Measurement & Geometry.w: V = (area of the circular base) × height = πr²h.

Measurement & Geometry.q: One cubic centimeter (cm³) holds how many milliliters?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 cm³ = 1 mL, so 1,000 cm³ = 1 L.

Measurement & Geometry.q: How many cubic feet are in 1 cubic yard?
Measurement & Geometry.w: 1 yd³ = 3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft = 27 ft³.

Measurement & Geometry.q: The three interior angles of any triangle add up to how many degrees?
Measurement & Geometry.w: Every triangle's interior angles sum to 180°.

Measurement & Geometry.q: In the Pythagorean theorem a² + b² = c², what does c represent?
Measurement & Geometry.w: c is the hypotenuse: the longest side, opposite the right angle.

Measurement & Geometry.q: Two angles are complementary when their measures add up to how many degrees?
Measurement & Geometry.w: Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary angles sum to 180°.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: In a two-way table, a question asks: 'Of the students who walk to school, what percent are seniors?' Which number belongs in the denominator?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The total number of students who walk
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: 'Of the students who walk' names the group you are taking a percent of, so the walkers' total is the denominator; seniors who walk is the numerator.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: On a line graph with evenly spaced time intervals, which segment shows the greatest rate of change?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The steepest segment, rising or falling
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Rate of change is the change in y per unit of x, which is shown by steepness. A steep fall is as large a change as a steep rise.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: In a stacked bar graph, how do you find the value of a segment in the middle of a bar?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: Subtract the value at its lower edge from the value at its upper edge
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Each segment starts where the one below it ends, so its value is top edge minus bottom edge.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: How do you find the central angle of a sector in a pie chart?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: Multiply the sector's percent as a decimal by 360°
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A full circle is 360°, so a sector's angle is its fraction of the whole times 360° (25% gives 0.25 x 360° = 90°).

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: In a histogram, what does the height of each bar show?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The number of data values that fall in that interval
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A histogram's bars cover intervals of a numeric variable, and the height is the frequency: how many values fall in the interval.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A stem-and-leaf plot has the key 6 | 3 = 63. Which values does the row 6 | 0 4 4 9 show?
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The stem is the tens digit and each leaf is a ones digit, and every leaf is a separate value: 60, 64, 64, 69.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: On a scatterplot, what does a negative correlation look like?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: Points that trend downward from left to right
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Negative correlation: as x increases, y tends to decrease, so the points drift downward from left to right.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: What does a strong correlation between two variables on a scatterplot show?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The points lie close to a single line
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Strength describes how tightly the points cluster around a line. Points close to the line show a strong correlation; widely scattered points show a weak one.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: What is it called when a trend line is used to predict a value far outside the range of the data, and how reliable is it?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: Extrapolation; it is less reliable
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Predicting beyond the data range is extrapolation; the trend may not continue there, so it is less reliable than interpolation within the range.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: How do you find the median of a data set with an even number of values?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: Order the values, then take the mean of the two middle values
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Always order the data first. With an even count there are two middle values, and the median is their mean (3, 5, 8, 10 gives 6.5).

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 12. What is the sum of the 5 numbers?
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Mean = sum / count, so sum = mean x count = 12 x 5 = 60.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: What is the mode of a data set?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The value that occurs most often
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The mode is the most frequent value. A data set can have no mode or more than one mode.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A distribution is skewed right. How do its mean and median usually compare?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The mean is greater than the median
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: In a right skew, a few large values form the tail on the right and pull the mean above the median.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Which two statistics are resistant to an outlier?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The median and the interquartile range
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The median and IQR depend on the middle of the ordered data, so one extreme value barely moves them. The mean and range are pulled by outliers.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: The same number is added to every value in a data set. What happens to the range?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: It stays the same
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The maximum and minimum both increase by the same amount, so their difference does not change. The mean, median and mode each increase by that number.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: On a graph of two related variables, which variable is usually plotted on the x-axis?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The independent variable
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: By convention the independent (input) variable goes on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent (output) variable on the vertical y-axis.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: In an experiment, what is the dependent variable?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The variable measured as the outcome
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The dependent variable is the response or outcome; its value depends on the independent variable.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: What is a controlled variable in an investigation?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: A factor kept the same in every trial
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Controlled variables are held constant so that any change in the outcome can be linked to the independent variable.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Which equation represents direct variation between x and y?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: y = 4x
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Direct variation has the form y = kx: the graph passes through the origin, and doubling x doubles y.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: In an inverse variation, y = k/x, what happens to y when x is doubled?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: y is halved
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The product xy stays equal to k, so if x doubles, y must be halved.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: In the linear equation y = mx + b, what does b represent?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: The value of y when x = 0
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: b is the y-intercept: the starting value of y when x = 0. The slope m is the rate of change.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at 80 instead of 0. What effect does this usually have on the graph?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: It makes the differences between bars look larger
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Cutting off the bottom of the axis removes the shared base of every bar, so small differences look large.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Which type of display is best for showing how one quantity changes over time?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: Line graph
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A line graph places time on the x-axis and connects the values in order, showing increases and decreases over time.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A picture graph shows an increase by doubling both the height and the width of an icon. How many times larger does the icon's area become?
Data, Statistics & Variables.a: 4 times
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Area scales by the product of the two factors: 2 x 2 = 4, so a doubling looks like a fourfold increase.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which level of organization comes directly above the tissue level?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Two or more tissue types working together form an organ, so the organ level sits directly above the tissue level.

A&P: Body Organization.q: An organ is built from at least how many tissue types?
A&P: Body Organization.w: An organ is two or more tissue types working together. Some organs, such as the stomach, contain all four.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Atoms and molecules make up which level of organization?
A&P: Body Organization.w: The chemical level, made of atoms and molecules, is the simplest level of structural organization.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which basic tissue type is the most abundant and widespread in the body?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Connective tissue is the most abundant and widespread tissue type, including bone, cartilage, blood, adipose and tendons.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which type of gland secretes its product through a duct onto a surface?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Exocrine glands, such as sweat and salivary glands, release secretions through ducts onto a surface.

A&P: Body Organization.q: In naming epithelium, what shape does "squamous" describe?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Squamous cells are flat; cuboidal cells are cube-shaped, and columnar cells are tall.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which directional term means toward the midline of the body?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Medial means toward the midline; lateral means away from it.

A&P: Body Organization.q: In human anatomy, dorsal is a synonym for which term?
A&P: Body Organization.w: In humans, dorsal means posterior (the back) and ventral means anterior (the front).

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which term describes structures on opposite sides of the body?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Contralateral means on the opposite side; ipsilateral means on the same side.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which plane divides the body into equal left and right halves?
A&P: Body Organization.w: The midsagittal (median) plane divides the body into equal left and right halves.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which abdominal quadrant contains the spleen?
A&P: Body Organization.w: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant, near the stomach.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The antecubital region, a common site for drawing blood, is located where?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Antecubital refers to the front of the elbow.

A&P: Body Organization.q: In a feedback loop, which component first detects a change in a variable?
A&P: Body Organization.w: The receptor (sensor) detects the change and sends the information to the control center.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which hormone drives the positive feedback loop of labor contractions?
A&P: Body Organization.w: Oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, which trigger more oxytocin release until delivery.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which brain structure acts as the control center for body temperature?
A&P: Body Organization.w: The hypothalamus compares body temperature with its set point and directs sweating or shivering.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which structure is the voice box, containing the vocal cords?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The larynx is the voice box; it contains the vocal cords and carries air only.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: How many lobes does the left lung have?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The left lung has 2 lobes (and a cardiac notch); the right lung has 3.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which cells in the alveolar wall secrete surfactant?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension in the alveoli.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which gas law explains why air flows into the lungs when the thoracic cavity enlarges?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, gas pressure and volume are inversely related, so a larger thorax means lower pressure and air flows in.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Vital capacity equals which sum of lung volumes?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Vital capacity = tidal volume (TV) + inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) + expiratory reserve volume (ERV).

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Is quiet expiration active or passive, and what mainly drives it?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.a: Passive; elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Quiet expiration is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the lungs and chest wall recoil elastically.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors that respond to rising carbon dioxide?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata detect the fall in cerebrospinal fluid pH caused by rising CO₂.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: What is the main form in which carbon dioxide is carried in the blood?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: About 70% of CO₂ travels as bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) in the plasma.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Prolonged hyperventilation causes which acid-base change?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, so less carbonic acid forms, H⁺ falls and pH rises: respiratory alkalosis.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which valve sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which layer lines the chambers of the heart and covers the valves?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The endocardium is the thin inner lining of the chambers and valves.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: What produces the second heart sound, S2 ("dub")?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: S2 is the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves closing at the start of diastole.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which chamber receives blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The venae cavae (and the coronary sinus) empty into the right atrium.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Into which chamber does the coronary sinus drain blood from the heart muscle?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Coronary veins drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which vessel carries nutrient-rich blood from the intestines to the liver?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas to the liver.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: What does the QRS complex on an ECG represent?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization, which triggers ventricular contraction.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which instrument is used with a cuff to measure blood pressure?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: A sphygmomanometer (blood pressure cuff and gauge) measures arterial blood pressure, usually at the brachial artery.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: What is the normal resting heart rate range for an adult?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: A normal adult resting heart rate is about 60 to 100 beats per minute, set by the SA node.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which formed elements are cell fragments from megakaryocytes that help form a clot?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Platelets (thrombocytes) are fragments of megakaryocytes; they form a platelet plug and support fibrin clotting.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which blood type is the universal recipient for red blood cells?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: AB positive has A, B and Rh (D) antigens and no anti-A, anti-B or anti-D antibodies, so it can receive red cells of any ABO/Rh type.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which layer of a blood vessel wall contains most of its smooth muscle?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic tissue.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: What is the wave-like contraction of smooth muscle that propels food along the digestive tract called?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Peristalsis is the wave-like smooth-muscle contraction that moves food along the tract, including the whole length of the esophagus.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: To which part of the large intestine is the appendix attached?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The appendix hangs from the cecum, the pouch-like first part of the large intestine.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: What is the semifluid mixture of partly digested food and gastric juice that leaves the stomach called?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The stomach churns food with gastric juice to form chyme, which the pyloric sphincter releases into the duodenum.
The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it and releases it in response to CCK.
Pancreatic lipase splits emulsified fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides in the small intestine.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which three pairs of major salivary glands secrete saliva into the mouth?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The three pairs of major salivary glands are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which enzyme in saliva begins the chemical digestion of starch?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Salivary amylase begins carbohydrate (starch) digestion in the mouth.
Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which hydrochloric acid converts into pepsin.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: What are the end products of protein digestion?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin and peptidases break proteins down to amino acids, which are absorbed into blood capillaries.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which region of the kidney contains the renal pyramids, with most loops of Henle and collecting ducts?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The renal medulla is made of renal pyramids, which hold the nephron loops and collecting ducts.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: What is the term for the act of emptying the urinary bladder?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Micturition is urination, controlled by a reflex plus voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which tube carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside; the ureters carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which process moves H⁺, K⁺, creatinine and some drugs from the blood into the renal tubule?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Tubular secretion moves substances from peritubular capillary blood into the filtrate, mainly in the PCT and DCT.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which part of the nephron loop is impermeable to water but pumps out Na⁺ and Cl⁻?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The ascending limb pumps out sodium and chloride while keeping water in, building the concentration gradient of the medulla.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: What is the main nitrogenous waste in urine, and where is it made?
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste in urine. The liver makes it from ammonia, and the kidneys excrete it.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which division of the peripheral nervous system carries information toward the central nervous system?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Afferent (sensory) fibers carry information toward the CNS; efferent (motor) fibers carry commands away from it.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves and spinal nerves make up the peripheral nervous system?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The PNS includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which autonomic division has thoracolumbar (T1 to L2) outflow and drives the fight-or-flight response?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The sympathetic division leaves the spinal cord from T1 to L2 and produces fight-or-flight responses.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: What are the small gaps between segments of the myelin sheath on an axon called?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Gaps in the myelin sheath are nodes of Ranvier; impulses jump from node to node (saltatory conduction).

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the CNS; glutamate is the main excitatory one.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Where on a neuron is the trigger zone at which action potentials begin?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The axon hillock, where the axon joins the cell body, is the trigger zone.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: List the meninges in order from the outermost layer to the innermost layer.
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Outer to inner: dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater (DAP).

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which structure connects the left and right cerebral hemispheres?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The corpus callosum is the band of white matter joining the two cerebral hemispheres.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which cranial nerve controls most eye movements and constriction of the pupil?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) controls most eye movement and constricts the pupil.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: What is the tough white outer layer of the eyeball called?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The sclera is the white outer layer of the eyeball.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Where are the hair cells that convert sound vibrations into nerve impulses?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Hair cells in the organ of Corti inside the cochlea convert vibrations into impulses carried by CN VIII.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which middle ear structure presses directly on the oval window?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The stapes, the last ossicle, pushes on the oval window of the cochlea.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which hormone is secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Alpha cells secrete glucagon; beta cells secrete insulin; delta cells secrete somatostatin.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates milk production?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which endocrine gland needs iodine to make its main hormones?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The thyroid needs iodine to make T3 and T4.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: What effect does calcitonin have on blood calcium levels?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.a: Lowers it by favoring bone deposition
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Calcitonin, from thyroid C cells, lowers blood calcium by favoring bone deposition and reducing osteoclast activity.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which receptors detect high plasma osmolality (dehydration) and trigger the release of ADH?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect high plasma osmolality and trigger ADH release and thirst.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Diabetes insipidus results from a lack of which hormone, or from kidney insensitivity to it?
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Diabetes insipidus is ADH deficiency or kidney insensitivity to ADH, causing large volumes of dilute urine.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which bone cells build new bone by secreting osteoid matrix?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Osteoblasts build bone (blasts build, clasts carve). Once trapped in the matrix they become osteocytes.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: What are the tiny channels that link osteocytes in neighboring lacunae?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Canaliculi are tiny channels that connect lacunae, letting osteocytes exchange nutrients and wastes.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: In an adult, where is most red bone marrow found?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.a: Spongy bone of flat bones and vertebrae
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Adult red marrow (hematopoiesis) is in spongy bone: flat bones such as the sternum and hip bones, vertebrae and the epiphyses of the femur and humerus.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which bone does not articulate with any other bone?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hyoid, in the neck, is held in place by muscles and ligaments and forms no joint with another bone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which vertebra has a dens that lets the head rotate from side to side?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The axis (C2) has the dens, a peg the atlas pivots around, allowing the side-to-side "no" rotation.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which is the longest and strongest bone in the human body?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which muscle group flexes the knee and extends the hip?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) flex the knee and extend the hip.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which muscle closes the jaw during chewing?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The masseter elevates the mandible, closing the jaw for chewing.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: What is the role of a muscle that opposes the prime mover by relaxing and stretching?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The antagonist opposes the agonist's action; it relaxes and stretches while the agonist contracts.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: What is the contractile unit of a myofibril, running from one Z disc to the next?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The sarcomere, from Z disc to Z disc, is the basic contractile unit of skeletal muscle.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During the cross-bridge cycle, what happens when ATP binds a myosin head?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: ATP binding releases the myosin head from actin; without ATP the heads stay attached (rigor mortis).

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.a: One motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: A motor unit is a single motor neuron plus every muscle fiber it innervates; recruiting more units increases force.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which protein makes keratinocytes tough and water-resistant?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Keratin is the tough, waterproofing protein that fills keratinocytes and the dead cells of the stratum corneum.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which layer beneath the dermis stores fat and is the site of subcutaneous injections?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) is adipose and areolar tissue that insulates, stores energy and anchors the skin.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which receptors in the dermal papillae detect light touch?
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Meissner (tactile) corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae of the papillary layer and detect light touch.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which male gland surrounds the urethra just below the urinary bladder?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The prostate surrounds the urethra just below the bladder and adds a milky, slightly acidic fluid containing enzymes such as PSA.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: In which structure do sperm mature and remain stored before ejaculation?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Sperm made in the seminiferous tubules move to the epididymis, where they mature and are stored.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which hypothalamic hormone triggers the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete FSH and LH.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates ovarian follicles to grow early in the cycle?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates follicle growth in the follicular phase.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which hormone stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production; oxytocin causes milk ejection.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which layer of the uterine wall has a functional layer that is shed during menstruation?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The endometrium lines the uterus; its functional layer is shed each menstrual phase and rebuilt in the proliferative phase.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which two organs are the primary lymphoid organs?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Red bone marrow (where lymphocytes form and B cells mature) and the thymus (where T cells mature) are the primary lymphoid organs.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which cells release histamine to start the inflammatory response?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Mast cells and basophils release histamine, causing vasodilation and increased capillary permeability.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Where are Peyer's patches, a type of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), found?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Peyer's patches are clusters of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the ileum of the small intestine.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which antibody class is made first in a primary immune response?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: IgM, a large pentamer, is the first antibody produced on first exposure to an antigen.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which antibody class is most abundant in tears, saliva, mucus and breast milk?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: IgA is the antibody of secretions, protecting mucous membranes; in breast milk it gives the infant passive immunity.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A vaccine gives which type of acquired immunity?
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: A vaccine is a medical intervention (artificial) that makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells (active).

Biology.q: Which type of cell lacks a membrane-bound nucleus?
Biology.w: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) keep their DNA in a nucleoid region with no nuclear membrane.

Biology.q: What is the main structural material of a plant cell wall?
Biology.w: Plant cell walls are built from the polysaccharide cellulose.

Biology.q: Which statement is one of the three tenets of cell theory?
Biology.a: All cells come from pre-existing cells.
Biology.w: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.

Biology.q: Which cell structure is the site of protein synthesis?
Biology.w: Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein, free in the cytoplasm or bound to rough ER.

Biology.q: Which organelle uses catalase to convert hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen?
Biology.w: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins, and their catalase turns H₂O₂ into water and O₂.

Biology.q: Which plant cell structure stores water and maintains turgor pressure?
Biology.w: The large central vacuole stores water, ions and wastes and keeps the cell turgid.

Biology.q: During osmosis, water moves toward which region?
Biology.a: The region of higher solute concentration
Biology.w: Water moves from lower solute (higher water) concentration to higher solute (lower water) concentration.

Biology.q: What happens to a red blood cell placed in a hypotonic solution?
Biology.w: Less solute outside means water enters by osmosis, so the cell swells and may lyse (hemolysis).

Biology.q: Which transport process moves a substance against its concentration gradient?
Biology.w: Active transport uses ATP and carrier proteins (pumps) to move substances from low to high concentration.

Biology.q: In which phase of mitosis do chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate?
Biology.w: Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the cell equator (metaphase plate).

Biology.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human egg or sperm cell?
Biology.w: Gametes are haploid (n): 23 chromosomes, half the diploid 46.

Biology.q: What does meiosis produce from one diploid parent cell?
Biology.w: Meiosis has two divisions and yields four genetically different haploid cells.

Biology.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
Biology.w: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen.

Biology.q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
Biology.w: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose (it uses 2 and makes 4).

Biology.q: Which molecule is the source of the oxygen gas released in photosynthesis?
Biology.w: Water is split in the light-dependent reactions, releasing O₂.

Biology.q: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with which base?
Biology.w: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds); G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds).

Biology.q: Which sugar is found in RNA nucleotides?
Biology.w: RNA contains ribose; DNA contains deoxyribose.

Biology.q: In eukaryotic cells, DNA wraps around which proteins to form chromatin?
Biology.w: DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which pack into chromatin and chromosomes.

Biology.q: How many mRNA bases make up one codon?
Biology.w: A codon is a triplet: 3 bases code for 1 amino acid.

Biology.q: Which mRNA codon is the start codon for translation?
Biology.w: AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine.

Biology.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does translation take place?
Biology.w: Translation happens at ribosomes, free in the cytoplasm or on the rough ER.

Biology.q: What phenotype ratio does a monohybrid cross Aa x Aa produce, with complete dominance?
Biology.w: Aa x Aa gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypes (genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa).

Biology.q: What term describes an individual with two identical alleles for a gene, such as BB or bb?
Biology.w: Homozygous = two identical alleles (BB or bb).

Biology.q: What phenotype ratio does the dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb produce, with complete dominance?
Biology.w: Two independently assorting heterozygous genes give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Biology.q: Type AB blood, in which both A and B antigens are expressed, is an example of which inheritance pattern?
Biology.w: IA and IB are codominant: both are fully expressed in an IAIB person.

Biology.q: Which genotype gives type O blood?
Biology.w: i is recessive to IA and IB, so type O requires ii.

Biology.q: Pink snapdragons (RW) are crossed with each other. What phenotype ratio do the offspring show?
Biology.w: With incomplete dominance the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio: 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW.

Biology.q: Which class of macromolecule provides the most energy per gram, about 9 kcal?
Biology.w: Lipids store about 9 kcal/g; carbohydrates and proteins give about 4 kcal/g.

Biology.q: What are the monomers of proteins?
Biology.w: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

Biology.q: Which polysaccharide forms plant cell walls and cannot be digested by humans?
Biology.w: Cellulose builds plant cell walls; humans lack the enzyme to digest it, so it acts as dietary fiber.

Biology.q: Which infectious agent is a misfolded protein that contains no DNA or RNA?
Biology.w: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

Biology.q: What does a typical virus particle consist of?
Biology.a: DNA or RNA inside a protein coat
Biology.w: A virus is nucleic acid (DNA or RNA, not both) in a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope.

Biology.q: Which organism is the vector that transmits Lyme disease?
Biology.w: Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) is spread by the bite of infected ticks.

Chemistry.q: What does the mass number of an atom count?
Chemistry.w: Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons, the particles in the nucleus. Neutrons = A - Z.

Chemistry.q: Which scientist discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model?
Chemistry.w: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron and pictured it embedded in a positive sphere (plum pudding).

Chemistry.q: Isotopes of the same element differ in their number of which particle?
Chemistry.w: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.

Chemistry.q: Elements in the same group (column) of the periodic table have the same number of what?
Chemistry.w: A group shares the same number of valence electrons, which gives its elements similar chemical properties.

Chemistry.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the first electron shell can hold?
Chemistry.w: Shell capacity is 2n squared: the first shell holds 2, the second 8 and the third 18.

Chemistry.q: Which group of the periodic table contains the noble gases?
Chemistry.w: Group 18 (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) has full outer shells, making these gases very unreactive.

Chemistry.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
Chemistry.w: Fluorine, at the upper right of the table (excluding noble gases), is the most electronegative element.

Chemistry.q: Moving down a group, how does atomic radius change?
Chemistry.w: Each step down a group adds an occupied electron shell, so atoms get larger.

Chemistry.q: Which family contains the most reactive metals?
Chemistry.w: Alkali metals have one valence electron that is easily lost, making them the most reactive metals.

Chemistry.q: What is the phase change from a gas directly to a solid called?
Chemistry.w: Deposition is gas to solid, as when frost forms; it releases heat.

Chemistry.q: At sea level (1 atm), at what temperature does pure water boil?
Chemistry.w: Pure water boils at 100 °C, 212 °F or 373 K at 1 atm.

Chemistry.q: Boyle's law relates which two quantities of a gas at constant temperature?
Chemistry.w: Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2; pressure and volume are inversely related.

Chemistry.q: What is the formula for density?
Chemistry.w: Density = mass / volume, often in g/mL or g/cm3.

Chemistry.q: Flammability is an example of which kind of property?
Chemistry.w: Flammability describes the ability to react (burn) and form new substances, so it is a chemical property.

Chemistry.q: Which of these is a compound?
Chemistry.w: Sodium chloride is two elements chemically combined in a fixed 1:1 ratio, which makes it a compound.

Chemistry.q: In a covalent bond, what do the atoms do with electrons?
Chemistry.w: Covalent bonds form when atoms, usually nonmetals, share pairs of electrons.

Chemistry.q: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen is bonded to which atoms?
Chemistry.w: Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen attached to a highly electronegative N, O or F atom.

Chemistry.q: Between two carbon atoms, which covalent bond is the strongest and shortest?
Chemistry.w: Bond strength rises from single to double to triple, and triple bonds are the shortest.

Chemistry.q: In a redox reaction, what does oxidation mean?
Chemistry.w: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain (OIL RIG).

Chemistry.q: Which pattern represents a synthesis reaction?
Chemistry.w: In synthesis, two or more reactants combine into a single product.

Chemistry.q: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
Chemistry.w: A hydrocarbon burned in enough oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water, plus energy.

Chemistry.q: What role do enzymes play in the body?
