Chemistry.w: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation energy and are not used up.

Chemistry.q: At chemical equilibrium, how do the forward and reverse reaction rates compare?
Chemistry.w: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

Chemistry.q: What is activation energy?
Chemistry.a: The minimum energy needed to start a reaction
Chemistry.w: Activation energy is the energy barrier colliding particles must overcome for a reaction to occur.

Chemistry.q: In salt water, which substance is the solvent?
Chemistry.w: The solvent does the dissolving and is present in the larger amount: water.

Chemistry.q: Molarity is defined as moles of solute per what?
Chemistry.w: Molarity (M) = moles of solute / liters of solution.

Chemistry.q: As temperature rises, what happens to the solubility of most solids in water?
Chemistry.w: Most solid solutes become more soluble as temperature rises; gases do the opposite.

Chemistry.q: At 25 °C, what pH value is neutral?
Chemistry.w: Pure water at 25 °C has pH 7: [H⁺] = [OH⁻].

Chemistry.q: In the Bronsted-Lowry definition, what is an acid?
Chemistry.w: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H+); a base accepts one.

Chemistry.q: What is the normal pH range of human arterial blood?
Chemistry.w: Normal blood pH is 7.35-7.45, slightly basic.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Which metric prefix means one-thousandth (10⁻³) of the base unit?
Which instrument measures an object's mass rather than its weight?
Scientific Reasoning.w: A balance compares an object against known masses, so it measures mass (grams). A spring scale measures force, which is weight (newtons).

Scientific Reasoning.q: One milliliter (1 mL) is equal to which volume?
Scientific Reasoning.w: 1 mL = 1 cm³ (also written 1 cc). One liter equals 1 cubic decimeter (1 dm³).

Scientific Reasoning.q: In measurement, what does accuracy describe?
Scientific Reasoning.a: How close a measurement is to the accepted value
Scientific Reasoning.w: Accuracy = closeness to the true or accepted value. Precision = closeness of repeated measurements to one another.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Which formula gives percent error? (Here "difference" means the absolute difference between the measured and accepted values.)
Scientific Reasoning.a: Difference divided by the accepted value, times 100
Scientific Reasoning.w: Percent error = |measured - accepted| / accepted x 100%. The difference is always compared with the accepted (true) value.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Repeating trials and averaging the results mainly reduces which kind of error?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Random error varies unpredictably in both directions, so averaging many trials lets the highs and lows cancel. It mainly affects precision.

Scientific Reasoning.q: At which temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same number?
Which formula converts a Celsius reading to Fahrenheit?
Scientific Reasoning.w: °F = (9/5 x °C) + 32. Multiply by 9/5 (1.8) first, then add 32.

Scientific Reasoning.q: In scientific notation, a × 10ⁿ, which range must the coefficient a fall in?
Scientific Reasoning.w: The coefficient must be at least 1 and less than 10: 1 <= a < 10 (for example 3.2 × 10⁻⁶).

Scientific Reasoning.q: In the scientific method, which step comes directly after forming a hypothesis?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Observation, question, research, hypothesis, then design and conduct an experiment to test it, followed by data analysis, conclusion and communication.

Scientific Reasoning.q: What does a scientific law do?
Scientific Reasoning.w: A law describes what consistently happens, often as a mathematical relationship (Boyle's law, conservation of mass), without explaining why.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Which form is a scientific hypothesis usually written in?
Scientific Reasoning.w: A hypothesis is a testable, tentative prediction or explanation, often written "If ... then ... because ...".

Scientific Reasoning.q: On a graph of experimental results, which variable is plotted on the x-axis?
Scientific Reasoning.w: DRY MIX: Dependent, Responding, Y-axis; Manipulated, Independent, X-axis.

Scientific Reasoning.q: In an experiment, what is the control group?
Scientific Reasoning.a: The group that receives no treatment or a placebo
Scientific Reasoning.w: The control group does not receive the treatment (or gets a placebo or standard condition) and is the baseline for comparison.

Scientific Reasoning.q: What does reliability mean in a scientific investigation?
Scientific Reasoning.a: Results are consistent across repeated trials
Scientific Reasoning.w: Reliability = consistency of results across repeated trials. Repeated trials and larger samples improve it.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Inductive reasoning moves in which direction?
Scientific Reasoning.a: From specific observations to a general rule
Scientific Reasoning.w: Inductive reasoning goes from specific observations to a general conclusion. Its conclusions are probable and can be overturned by one counterexample.

Scientific Reasoning.q: In science, what is an inference?
Scientific Reasoning.w: An inference interprets observations ("the plant lacks nitrogen"); an observation is what is directly seen or measured ("the leaf is yellow").

Scientific Reasoning.q: Which type of study can establish cause and effect?
Scientific Reasoning.w: A controlled experiment changes one variable and holds the others constant, so it can show cause and effect.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Which type of estimate from data is more reliable, and why?
Scientific Reasoning.a: Interpolation, as it estimates between measured points
Scientific Reasoning.w: Interpolation estimates between measured points, inside the range tested, so it is more reliable than extrapolation, which assumes the trend continues beyond the data.

Scientific Reasoning.q: On a graph, how does an inverse relationship between two variables appear?
Scientific Reasoning.a: A line sloping downward from left to right
Scientific Reasoning.w: In an inverse (negative) relationship, y falls as x rises, so the line or curve slopes downward from left to right.

Scientific Reasoning.q: One bacterial cell divides by binary fission. How many cells are present after n generations?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Each generation doubles the count (1, 2, 4, 8 ...), so after n generations there are 2ⁿ cells: exponential growth.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which is the one common English word that ends in -sede?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Supersede is the only common -sede word. Exceed, proceed and succeed end in -ceed; the rest end in -cede.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Following the silent-e rule, which pair of words is spelled correctly?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Drop the silent e before a vowel suffix (hoping) and keep it before a consonant suffix (hopeful).

Conventions of Standard English.q: Applying the final-y rule, what is the correct spelling when -ing is added to "study"?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Consonant + y changes y to i before most suffixes, but the y is kept before -ing: studying.

Conventions of Standard English.q: What is the correct plural possessive of "child"?
Conventions of Standard English.w: The plural is the irregular "children", which does not end in s, so the possessive adds 's.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which noun has the same form in the singular and the plural?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Species, like deer, sheep, series and aircraft, does not change in the plural.

Conventions of Standard English.q: How do you show that two named people own one thing together?
Conventions of Standard English.a: Add 's to the last name only
Conventions of Standard English.w: Joint ownership: last name only (Maria and Lee's clinic). Individual ownership: each name (Maria's and Lee's cars).

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which word is usually a verb meaning "to influence"?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Affect = to influence (verb). Effect = result (noun), or as a verb, to bring about.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which word means "staff" or "employees"?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Personnel = staff. Personal = private or relating to a person.

Conventions of Standard English.q: "It's" is a contraction of which words?
Conventions of Standard English.w: It's = it is (It's late) or it has (It's been a long day). The possessive is its, with no apostrophe.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which list contains only coordinating conjunctions?
Conventions of Standard English.a: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
Conventions of Standard English.w: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. With a comma before them, they join independent clauses.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which kind of clause is set off with commas?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Nonessential clauses add extra information and are enclosed in commas. Essential clauses identify the noun and take no commas.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A full date such as July 4, 2026, appears in the middle of a sentence. Where do the commas go?
Conventions of Standard English.a: After the day and after the year
Conventions of Standard English.w: On July 4, 2026, the clinic opened: commas follow the day and the year.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Two independent clauses are joined by "however." How is the sentence punctuated?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Clause; however, clause. The semicolon joins the clauses and the comma follows the conjunctive adverb.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A colon that introduces a list must follow what?
Conventions of Standard English.w: The words before a colon must be able to stand alone as a sentence.

Conventions of Standard English.q: What do brackets mark inside a quotation?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Brackets enclose the writer's own clarifying insertions, such as "He [the patient] refused."

Conventions of Standard English.q: In US style, where do periods and commas go with a closing quotation mark?
Conventions of Standard English.w: US style puts periods and commas inside closing quotation marks every time.

Conventions of Standard English.q: In US style, where do semicolons and colons go with a closing quotation mark?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Semicolons and colons go outside closing quotation marks; only periods and commas go inside.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which kind of title belongs in quotation marks?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Short works (stories, poems, articles, songs, chapters) take quotation marks; long works are italicized.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which word should be capitalized in a sentence?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Days of the week are proper nouns. Seasons, general subjects and compass directions are lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: When is a family word such as "mom" capitalized?
Conventions of Standard English.a: When it is used as a name
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Ask Mom" (used as a name) is capitalized; "my mom" (after a possessive) is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: In a title written in title case, which word is normally lowercase when it appears in the middle?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Short prepositions, articles and coordinating conjunctions are lowercase in the middle of a title. Verbs (is), pronouns (it) and adverbs (not) are capitalized.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which clause pattern defines a compound-complex sentence?
Conventions of Standard English.a: Two or more independent clauses plus a dependent clause
Conventions of Standard English.w: Compound-complex = two or more independent clauses + at least one dependent clause.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which sentence type gives a command or makes a request?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Imperative sentences command or request, with "you" understood as the subject.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which word, placed at the start of a clause, makes that clause dependent?
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Because" is a subordinating conjunction, so the clause it begins cannot stand alone.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Subordinating conjunctions (although, because, when, if, since, unless) begin dependent clauses.

Conventions of Standard English.q: What is a group of related words that lacks a subject-verb pair?
Conventions of Standard English.w: A phrase has no subject-verb pair; a clause has both.

Conventions of Standard English.q: In "Swimming is good exercise," which kind of verbal is "Swimming"?
Conventions of Standard English.w: An -ing verbal used as a noun (here, the subject) is a gerund.

Conventions of Standard English.q: What is formed when two independent clauses are joined by only a comma?
Conventions of Standard English.w: Clause, clause. = comma splice. With no punctuation at all, it is a fused (run-on) sentence.

Conventions of Standard English.q: What is a dependent clause that stands alone as if it were a sentence?
Conventions of Standard English.w: A dependent clause cannot stand alone; punctuated as a sentence, it is a fragment.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which punctuation mark alone can correctly join two independent clauses?
Conventions of Standard English.w: A semicolon can join two independent clauses without a conjunction. A comma needs a coordinating conjunction with it.

Knowledge of Language.q: With "neither...nor" or "either...or," the verb agrees with which part of the subject?
Knowledge of Language.a: The subject nearer to the verb
Knowledge of Language.w: The proximity rule: the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. "Neither the doctor nor the nurses are"; "Neither the nurses nor the doctor is."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which indefinite pronoun can take either a singular or a plural verb, depending on the noun it refers to?
Knowledge of Language.w: Some, any, none, all, most and more depend on the noun: "Most of the water is gone" but "Most of the samples are labeled."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence "The number of open beds ___ dropped this week"?
Knowledge of Language.w: "The number of" is singular ("has"); "a number of" means "several" and is plural ("A number of beds have opened").

Knowledge of Language.q: Which pronoun case is used for the object of a preposition such as "to," "for" or "between"?
Knowledge of Language.w: Objects of verbs and prepositions take the objective case: "for Maria and me," "between you and me," "to him."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which test helps you choose between "who" and "whom"?
Knowledge of Language.a: Swap in he or him: he = who, him = whom
Knowledge of Language.w: Who is subjective (like he); whom is objective (like him). "Whom did you call?" (you called him). "Who is calling?" (he is calling).

Knowledge of Language.q: When is a reflexive pronoun such as "myself" used correctly?
Knowledge of Language.a: When its antecedent is in the same clause
Knowledge of Language.w: "I hurt myself" is correct because "I" is in the same clause. A reflexive can also add emphasis ("I did it myself"), but it never replaces "me" or "I" on its own.

Knowledge of Language.q: What is the past participle of "lie" meaning "to recline"?
Knowledge of Language.w: Lie (recline): lie, lay, lain. Lay (put down): lay, laid, laid.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which tense shows that one past action was completed before another past action?
Knowledge of Language.w: "She had left before the doctor arrived": had left (earlier), arrived (later).

Knowledge of Language.q: What are the simple past and past participle of "begin"?
Knowledge of Language.w: Begin, began, begun: "The shift began at 7." "The shift has begun."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which word goes with a countable plural noun such as "patients"?
Knowledge of Language.w: Fewer patients, fewer errors; less water, less pain.

Knowledge of Language.q: "Running to catch the bus, my backpack ripped." What error does this sentence contain?
Knowledge of Language.w: The backpack cannot run. The person running must follow the comma: "Running to catch the bus, I ripped my backpack."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which form of an adjective is used when comparing exactly two items?
Knowledge of Language.w: Two items: better, taller, more careful. Three or more: best, tallest, most careful.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which word is a concise replacement for the phrase "due to the fact that"?
Knowledge of Language.w: Wordy phrases have short equivalents: due to the fact that = because; in order to = to; at this point in time = now.

Knowledge of Language.q: After a correlative pair such as "neither...nor," what must the two elements share?
Knowledge of Language.w: Both...and, either...or, neither...nor and not only...but also each introduce elements in matching form: "neither for patients nor for staff."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which phrase is redundant?
Knowledge of Language.w: History is always in the past, so "past history" repeats an idea. Similar redundancies: end result, free gift, close proximity, repeat again.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which feature is typical of formal academic writing?
Knowledge of Language.w: Formal writing uses complete sentences, precise words, standard grammar, an objective tone and few or no contractions.

Knowledge of Language.q: For a patient handout read by the general public, which term is best?
Knowledge of Language.w: Plain language uses everyday words for lay readers: "high blood pressure" rather than "hypertension."

Knowledge of Language.q: Which three elements make up a rhetorical context?
Knowledge of Language.w: Rhetorical context = why you are writing (purpose), who will read it (audience) and the setting or medium (occasion).

Knowledge of Language.q: Which phrase uses person-first language?
Knowledge of Language.w: Person-first language puts the person before the condition: a person with asthma, a patient who uses a wheelchair.

Knowledge of Language.q: What is specialized vocabulary that experts understand but general readers may not?
Knowledge of Language.w: Jargon suits specialists (a report to clinicians) but should be replaced with plain words for general readers.

Knowledge of Language.q: What is an overused expression such as "think outside the box" called?
Knowledge of Language.w: Clichés are tired phrases (at the end of the day, a walk in the park). Replace them with specific statements.

Knowledge of Language.q: What is the role of a topic sentence?
Knowledge of Language.a: It states the paragraph's main idea
Knowledge of Language.w: The topic sentence states the main idea, usually at the start of the paragraph; every other sentence supports it.

Knowledge of Language.q: A paragraph has unity when which condition is met?
Knowledge of Language.a: Every sentence relates to the main idea
Knowledge of Language.w: Unity means every sentence supports the topic sentence; an off-topic sentence should be removed.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which organizational pattern presents events in the order in which they happened?
Knowledge of Language.w: Chronological (time) order follows events as they happened, often signaled by first, next, then and finally.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which transition signals contrast?
Knowledge of Language.w: Contrast transitions include however, nevertheless, nonetheless, on the other hand, in contrast and conversely.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which transition signals a result?
Knowledge of Language.w: Cause-and-effect transitions include therefore, thus, consequently, as a result and hence.

Knowledge of Language.q: Which transition introduces an example?
Knowledge of Language.w: Example transitions include for example, for instance, such as, to illustrate and specifically.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which stage of the writing process focuses on content and organization rather than sentence-level correctness?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Revising improves the big picture: thesis, order, support and relevance (add, rearrange, remove, replace).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which prewriting technique arranges ideas in a formal hierarchy labeled with Roman numerals, capital letters, and numbers?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A formal outline orders ideas as main points and subpoints, labeled I., A., 1., a.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which stage of the writing process comes directly after drafting?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: The order is prewriting, drafting, revising, editing (with proofreading), publishing.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which is a feature of an effective thesis statement?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.a: It makes a specific, arguable claim
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A thesis is one sentence stating a specific, focused, arguable main claim.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: In a formal outline, which label comes directly beneath a main point labeled II.?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Outline levels run I., A., 1., a., so the first point under II. is A.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Correcting a misspelled word in a draft belongs to which stage of the writing process?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Editing (including the final proofread) fixes spelling, grammar, usage and punctuation.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which citation style is most commonly required in nursing programs?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: APA (author-date) is standard in nursing and the social sciences.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What is a cited restatement of a source's main ideas, in your own words and much shorter than the original?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A summary gives only the main ideas, in your own words, and is much shorter; it still needs a citation.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which kind of information can a writer use without a citation?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Widely known, undisputed facts (common knowledge) need no citation.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the prefix tachy- mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: tachy- means fast, as in tachycardia (a fast heart rate).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the prefix inter- mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: inter- means between, as in intercostal (between the ribs).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the prefix dys- mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: dys- means bad, difficult or painful, as in dyspnea (difficult breathing).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the root rupt mean, as in rupture?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: rupt means break: a rupture is a break or burst.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the root spect mean, as in inspect?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: spec/spect means look: to inspect is to look closely.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the root bene mean, as in benefit?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: bene means good or well, as in benefit and benign.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the suffix -ectomy mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: -ectomy means surgical removal, as in appendectomy.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the suffix -algia mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: -algia (like -dynia) means pain, as in neuralgia.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which suffix means inflammation?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: -itis means inflammation, as in arthritis and gastritis.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which combining form means kidney?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: nephr/o (and ren/o) means kidney, as in nephrology.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the combining form oste/o mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: oste/o means bone, as in osteoporosis.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which combining form means white?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: leuk/o means white, as in leukocyte (white blood cell).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the prefix in- mean in the word inaudible?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: In inaudible, in- means not: not able to be heard.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the prefix retro- mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: retro- means backward or behind, as in retroperitoneal and retrospective.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: What does the prefix homo- (or homeo-) mean?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: homo-/homeo- means same or similar, as in homeostasis and homogeneous.
